title: Night Owls Are Not Just Tired. They Are Lonelier, More Anxious, and Science Now Knows Why.
excerpt: A new study presented at SLEEP 2026 found that 'nocturnal loneliness' — the isolation of being awake while the world sleeps — may be the hidden driver of anxiety in late sleepers. For first-gen immigrants working across time zones, the finding hits close to home.
body:
Everyone knows a night owl. In Indian families, it is often the uncle replying to WhatsApp messages at 1 AM, the tech worker on a late call with Bangalore, or the college student doom-scrolling long after the house has gone dark. Being a late sleeper has always been treated as a personality quirk — harmless, maybe even romantic. New research presented at one of the world's largest sleep conferences suggests it is neither.

A study from Brigham Young University, set to be formally presented at the SLEEP 2026 annual meeting in Baltimore, has identified a previously overlooked mechanism linking late sleep schedules to poorer mental health. The researchers call it "nocturnal loneliness" — the specific feeling of isolation, disconnection, and emotional exposure that strikes when someone is awake while most of the world around them is asleep.

The study examined 442 adults and measured three things: their natural sleep timing preference (known as chronotype), their levels of loneliness, and their anxiety symptoms. The results were clear. Evening chronotypes — people who naturally prefer later bedtimes and wake-up times — reported consistently higher levels of both loneliness and anxiety than their morning-oriented peers.

The Mechanism Nobody Was Studying

The most important discovery was not the correlation itself. Researchers have known for years that night owls tend to report worse mental health. What the BYU team found was why.

When they included nocturnal loneliness in their statistical model, the direct connection between late chronotype and anxiety became statistically insignificant. In plain terms: being a night owl does not inherently cause anxiety. But being awake alone at 2 AM — when businesses are closed, friends are asleep, social media goes quiet, and the world feels genuinely empty — does.

This distinction matters because it points to a solvable problem rather than an innate flaw. If the loneliness of nighttime is the real driver, then addressing that loneliness could break the cycle.

The Diaspora Dimension

For South Asians in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, this finding carries particular weight. The diaspora's relationship with late nights is not simply a matter of preference — it is often structural.

First-generation immigrants frequently work across time zones. A software engineer in San Jose might spend evenings on calls with teams in Hyderabad or Pune, finishing work at midnight and winding down well past 1 AM. A small business owner may close shop late and find themselves eating dinner alone at 11 PM. These are not people who choose to be night owls. Their lives demand it.

The social infrastructure compounds the problem. In India, late nights come with built-in company — chai stalls are open past midnight, neighbours drop by unannounced, streets remain alive. In American suburbs, the house goes quiet by 9 PM. The mismatch between the social rhythms someone grew up with and the environment they now live in creates exactly the kind of nocturnal isolation the BYU researchers identified.

Add to this the well-documented reluctance among South Asians to seek mental health support. A study published earlier this year found that Asian Americans use anxiety medication at half the rate of white Americans, with barriers that go far deeper than stigma alone. The result is a population that is simultaneously more exposed to nocturnal loneliness and less likely to address its consequences.

What Can Actually Help

The researchers believe their findings have practical implications. If nocturnal loneliness is the bridge between late sleep and anxiety, interventions do not need to force people into earlier bedtimes — an approach that often fails because chronotype has a strong genetic component.

Instead, the focus should shift to what happens during those late hours. Meaningful social connection in the evening — even asynchronous ones like voice notes to friends in other time zones, online communities, or scheduled late-night video calls — can reduce the sense of isolation. Structured evening routines that include something beyond screens may also help.

Healthcare providers, the researchers suggest, should ask patients not just how much they sleep but how they feel during the hours before sleep. The quality of those waking hours may matter as much as the sleep itself.

For a diaspora community that has normalised late nights as a feature of ambition and cross-border connection, the study offers a quiet warning: it is not the staying up that costs you. It is the staying up alone.
